papers.conclusion: Angular Steering offers a principled, flexible, and robust framework for behavior control in LLMs, enabling fine-grained modulation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors like refusal and compliance by rotating activations in a fixed 2D subspace.
The method generalizes existing activation addition and directional ablation techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework.
Angular Steering maintains general language modeling performance (e.g., on TINYBENCHMARKS) while effectively steering behavior.
Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant, improves robustness and coherence by rotating only activations aligned with the target feature.
Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show the method's flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches.
papers.limitation: The method requires a contrastive dataset to extract the feature direction, which may not always be available.
future_direction: Extending Angular Steering to multi-feature steering and dynamic plane selection.
papers.abstract: Controlling specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities is a central challenge for safe and reliable artificial intelligence deployment. Current steering methods, such as vector addition and directional ablation, are constrained within a two-dimensional subspace defined by the activation and feature direction, making them sensitive to chosen parameters and potentially affecting unrelated features due to unintended interactions in activation space. We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace. By formulating steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors such as refusal and compliance. We demonstrate this method using refusal steering emotion steering as use cases. Additionally, we propose Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant that rotates only activations aligned with the target feature, further enhancing stability and coherence. Angular Steering generalizes existing addition and orthogonalization techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework, simplifying parameter selection and maintaining model stability across a broader range of adjustments. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show that Angular Steering achieves robust behavioral control while maintaining general language modeling performance, underscoring its flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/lone17/angular-steering/.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: The Information Geometry of Softmax: Probing and Steering
papers.research_question: How do AI systems encode semantic structure into the geometric structure of their representation spaces, and how can the information geometry of softmax-based models be used for robust concept steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dual steering, a method that uses information geometry to robustly steer representations in softmax-based models, optimally modifying the target concept while minimizing changes to off-target concepts.
papers.conclusion: The non-Euclidean structure of the intrinsic information geometry of representation vectors is critical for connecting geometry and semantic tasks such as steering, and dual steering provides a robust method for concept manipulation in softmax-based models.
papers.key_findings:
The natural geometry for softmax representation spaces is information geometry, which is critical for connecting geometry and semantic tasks.
Dual steering, derived from information geometry, optimally modifies the target concept while minimizing off-target changes, as proven theoretically.
Empirical results on Gemma-3-4B and MetaClip-2 show dual steering outperforms Euclidean steering in preserving off-target distributions.
The duality structure of information geometry reveals distinct primal and dual interpolations with different semantic behaviors (AND-like vs OR-like).
The probing assumption (concept probability constant along a hyperplane) is stringent and may not hold in practice, affecting steering performance.
papers.limitation:
The probing assumption that the concept probability is constant along the hyperplane defined by the linear probe is stringent and may not hold in practice, which can affect the performance of dual steering.
The method is currently applied to the parameter space of the softmax layer; extending the geometry analysis to intermediate layers is an important future direction.
future_direction: Extending the geometry analysis to intermediate layers within the model.
Understanding how the geometry of the softmax layer and of attention layers influences the geometry of intermediate layers.
papers.abstract: This paper concerns the question of how AI systems encode semantic structure into the geometric structure of their representation spaces. The motivating observation of this paper is that the natural geometry of these representation spaces should reflect the way models use representations to produce behavior. We focus on the important special case of representations that define softmax distributions. In this case, we argue that the natural geometry is information geometry. Our focus is on the role of information geometry on semantic encoding and the linear representation hypothesis. As an illustrative application, we develop "dual steering", a method for robustly steering representations to exhibit a particular concept using linear probes. We prove that dual steering optimally modifies the target concept while minimizing changes to off-target concepts. Empirically, we find that dual steering enhances the controllability and stability of concept manipulation.

papers.title: LinEAS: End-to-end Learning of Activation Steering with a Distributional Loss
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently control generative models by steering activations with a global distributional loss that requires low data and is modality-agnostic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LinEAS, a method for activation steering that uses a global distributional loss to jointly learn affine transformations across layers, enabling effective control with low data and automatic neuron selection via sparsity regularization.
papers.conclusion: LinEAS is an effective method for activation steering, offering improved controllability and robustness by learning lightweight interventions with a global distributional loss.
papers.key_findings:
LinEAS outperforms existing activation steering methods on toxicity mitigation in LLMs and style control in text-to-image models.
LinEAS requires only a handful of unpaired samples (e.g., 32) to be effective.
The global loss and joint optimization across layers lead to more robust interventions and better preservation of model utility.
Sparsity regularization allows automatic selection of neurons and layers, reducing the intervention support by 100x.
LinEAS provides a continuous intervention strength parameter, allowing fine-grained control.
papers.limitation: The method requires access to intermediate activations, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending LinEAS to other modalities and tasks.
Investigating the theoretical properties of the distributional loss.
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative models in daily life calls for efficient mechanisms to control their generation, to e.g., produce safe content or provide users with tools to explore style changes. Ideally, such mechanisms should require low volume of unpaired data (i.e., without explicit preference), and should be cheap, both at train and inference time, while preserving output quality. Recent research has shown that such mechanisms can be obtained by intervening exclusively on model activations, with the goal of correcting distributional differences between activations seen when using prompts from a source vs. a target set (e.g., toxic and non-toxic sentences). While cheap, these fast methods are inherently crude: their maps are tuned locally, not accounting for their impact on downstream layers, resulting in interventions that cause unintended shifts when used out-of-sample. We propose in this work linear end-to-end activation steering (LinEAS), an approach trained with a global loss that accounts simultaneously for all layer-wise distributional shifts. In addition to being more robust, the loss used to train LinEAS can be regularized with sparsifying norms, which can automatically carry out neuron selection. LinEAS only requires a handful of unpaired samples to be effective, and beats similar baselines on toxicity mitigation in language models, becoming competitive with oracle-dependent methods that have access to strong supervision. LinEAS is modality-agnostic and we empirically find that it outperforms existing activation steering methods at mitigating and including new concepts at the output of single-step text-to-image generation models.

papers.title: Does higher interpretability imply better utility? A Pairwise Analysis on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does higher interpretability of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features imply better steering utility for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds only a weak positive association between SAE feature interpretability and steering utility, and introduces a new feature selection criterion (∆Token Confidence) that significantly improves steering performance.
papers.conclusion: There is a significant divergence between SAE interpretability and steering utility, suggesting that prioritizing interpretability does not guarantee improved steering performance.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability shows a relatively weak positive association with steering utility (Kendall's τb ≈ 0.298).
∆Token Confidence effectively selects features with strong steering performance, improving steering score by 52.52% over the previous best method.
After selecting high-utility features with ∆Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes or becomes negative.
future_direction: Developing advanced post-training feature selection protocols or fundamentally new, utility-oriented SAE training paradigms.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to steer large language models (LLMs), based on the assumption that their interpretable features naturally enable effective model behavior steering. Yet, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does higher interpretability indeed imply better steering utility? To answer this question, we train 90 SAEs across three LLMs (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Gemma-2-9B), spanning five architectures and six sparsity levels, and evaluate their interpretability and steering utility based on SAEBench (arXiv:2501.12345) and AxBench (arXiv:2502.23456) respectively, and perform a rank-agreement analysis via Kendall's rank coefficients (tau b). Our analysis reveals only a relatively weak positive association (tau b approx 0.298), indicating that interpretability is an insufficient proxy for steering performance. We conjecture the interpretability utility gap may stem from the selection of SAE features, as not all of them are equally effective for steering. To further find features that truly steer the behavior of LLMs, we propose a novel selection criterion called Delta Token Confidence, which measures how much amplifying a feature changes the next token distribution. We show that our method improves the steering performance of three LLMs by 52.52 percent compared to the current best output score based criterion (arXiv:2503.34567). Strikingly, after selecting features with high Delta Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes (tau b approx 0), and can even become negative. This further highlights the divergence between interpretability and utility for the most effective steering features.

papers.title: Understanding How CodeLLMs (Mis)Predict Types with Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Why do type mispredictions occur in CodeLLMs? The paper investigates whether models learn robust internal mechanisms for type prediction that fail to activate in adversarial scenarios.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs have a robust internal mechanism for type prediction which can be activated via activation steering, and that this mechanism is shared across programming languages.
papers.conclusion: There exists a robust mechanism for type prediction in LLMs which, when activated through activation steering, is more robust against adversarial programs and generalizes across languages.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering significantly improves type prediction accuracy on adversarial tasks where models initially fail.
The type prediction mechanism identified via steering is shared between Python and TypeScript, indicating language-agnostic representations.
Steering outperforms in-context learning for correcting type mispredictions.
Steering enables correct type prediction but does not improve the precision of the predicted types (e.g., from 'any' to a more specific type).
The type prediction mechanism spans several adjacent layers in the transformer, with steering on five layers being most effective.
papers.limitation: Steering enables type prediction but does not improve type precision (e.g., it does not make imprecise types like 'any' more precise).
future_direction: Investigating whether it is possible to identify a mechanism in LLMs that controls the degree of type precision.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used by software engineers for programming tasks. However, research shows that LLMs often lack a deep understanding of program semantics. Even minor changes to syntax, such as renaming variables, can significantly degrade performance across various tasks. In this work, we examine the task of type prediction: given a partially typed program, can a model predict a missing type annotations such that the resulting program is more typed? We construct a dataset of adversarial examples where models initially predict the correct types, but begin to fail after semantically irrelevant edits. This is problematic, as models should ideally generalize across different syntactic forms of semantically equivalent code. This lack of robustness suggests that models may have a shallow understanding of code semantics. Despite this, we provide evidence that LLMs do, in fact, learn robust mechanisms for type prediction-though these mechanisms often fail to activate in adversarial scenarios. By using activation steering, a method that manipulates a model's internal activations to guide it toward using latent knowledge, we restore accurate predictions on adversarial inputs. We show that steering successfully activates a type prediction mechanism that is shared by both Python and TypeScript, and is more effective than prompting with in-context examples. Across five different models, our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that LLMs can learn generalizable representations of code semantics that transfer across programming languages.

papers.title: Steering Conceptual Bias via Transformer Latent-Subspace Activation
papers.research_question: Can activating latent subspaces in language models steer scientific code generation toward a specific programming language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces G-ACT, a gradient-refined adaptive activation steering framework that uses per-layer probes to reliably steer LLM code generation towards a target programming language (e.g., CPP) with minimal runtime overhead.
papers.conclusion: G-ACT provides a scalable, interpretable, and efficient mechanism for steering LLMs toward a target concept (like CPP code) with acceptable inference costs and enables reproducible model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Static neuron attribution can bias language selection but is brittle and sensitive to neuron choice and prompt formulation.
G-ACT improves probe classification accuracy and macro-F1, especially in early layers (e.g., from 0% to 61.5% in layers 0-6 for LLaMA-3.2 3B).
G-ACT is scalable and works even in large models (70B) where attention signals become diffuse.
The method incurs a modest runtime overhead (approx. 1.3-1.4x slower than base generation) but remains practical by steering only a subset of layers.
papers.limitation:
Static neuron-attribution method is brittle, with performance highly sensitive to choice of neuron, prompt formulation, and model scale.
Per-layer probing introduces a modest runtime overhead (approximately 1.3–1.4× slower than base generation).
papers.abstract: This work examines whether activating latent subspaces in language models (LLMs) can steer scientific code generation toward a specific programming language. Five causal LLMs were first evaluated on scientific coding prompts to quantify their baseline bias among four programming languages. A static neuron-attribution method, perturbing the highest activated MLP weight for a C++ or CPP token, proved brittle and exhibited limited generalization across prompt styles and model scales. To address these limitations, a gradient-refined adaptive activation steering framework (G-ACT) was developed: per-prompt activation differences are clustered into a small set of steering directions, and lightweight per-layer probes are trained and refined online to select the appropriate steering vector. In LLaMA-3.2 3B, this approach reliably biases generation towards the CPP language by increasing the average probe classification accuracy by 15% and the early layers (0-6) improving the probe classification accuracy by 61.5% compared to the standard ACT framework. For LLaMA-3.3 70B, where attention-head signals become more diffuse, targeted injections at key layers still improve language selection. Although per-layer probing introduces a modest inference overhead, it remains practical by steering only a subset of layers and enables reproducible model behavior. These results demonstrate a scalable, interpretable and efficient mechanism for concept-level control for practical agentic systems.

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret the internal representations of protein language models and steer them to generate sequences with desired features?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can be applied to protein language models to interpret their internal representations and that the identified latent features can be used to steer the model to generate protein sequences with desired structural motifs.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders provide a promising approach for interpreting and controlling protein language models, opening new avenues for protein design and engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders trained on ESM-2 activations can identify latent components associated with protein annotations such as transmembrane regions, binding sites, and zinc finger motifs.
A heuristic based on intrinsic dimension estimation can guide the selection of the transformer layer from which to extract representations for SAE training.
Intervening on specific latent components during inference can steer the model to generate protein sequences that contain desired features, such as zinc finger domains.
The sequence generation pipeline successfully produced sequences with zinc finger motifs, though it requires parameter tuning to improve success rates.
papers.limitation:
The sequence generation pipeline requires parameter fine-tuning to improve the success rate.
The features learned by the model may not directly align with manually curated dataset annotations, as latents might encode more specific or coarse-grained features.
future_direction: Extend these methods to larger models and a wider range of protein features.
Automate the parameter search for the sequence generation pipeline to improve efficiency.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancements in transformer-based language models have revolutionized natural language processing, yet understanding the internal mechanisms of these models remains a significant challenge. This paper explores the application of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to interpret the internal representations of protein language models, specifically focusing on the ESM-2 8M parameter model. By performing a statistical analysis on each latent component's relevance to distinct protein annotations, we identify potential interpretations linked to various protein characteristics, including transmembrane regions, binding sites, and specialized motifs. We then leverage these insights to guide sequence generation, shortlisting the relevant latent components that can steer the model towards desired targets such as zinc finger domains. This work contributes to the emerging field of mechanistic interpretability in biological sequence models, offering new perspectives on model steering for sequence design.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do various representation-based steering methods compare to prompting and finetuning in terms of concept detection and model steering for language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AXBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating steering and concept detection methods, and finds that prompting outperforms representation-based methods for steering, while difference-in-means and probes are best for detection, with the novel ReFT-r1 method being competitive on both tasks.
papers.conclusion: Representation steering methods largely lag behind prompting and finetuning, but ReFT-r1 shows that steering can be improved with comprehensive benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting is the best method for model steering, outperforming all representation-based methods.
Difference-in-means, linear probes, and ReFT-r1 perform best for concept detection with no significant difference between them.
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are not competitive compared to other methods on both steering and detection.
ReFT-r1, a novel weakly-supervised method, is competitive on both steering and detection tasks while offering interpretability advantages.
The AXBENCH benchmark enables comprehensive evaluation and comparison of steering methods.
papers.limitation: Hyperparameter tuning might underestimate steering performance due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Extend AXBENCH to arbitrary concept descriptions and add new evaluation tasks as better feature-labelling techniques and steering approaches emerge.
papers.abstract: Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals, but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs), linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning; ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does a transparent algorithm constitute a faithful interpretation of the known, but opaque, low-level details of a black box model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper generalizes the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement to arbitrary mechanism transformation, and uses this framework to provide a flexible, precise formalization for core mechanistic interpretability concepts (polysemantic neurons, linear representation hypothesis, modular features, graded faithfulness) and to unify a wide range of existing interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction provides a solid theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, enabling precise definitions of core concepts and a unified perspective on existing methods, which facilitates rigorous falsification through experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
Causal abstraction theory is generalized to allow for arbitrary mechanism transformations (interventionals), which enables the isolation of quantities distributed across overlapping sets of microvariables.
The core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness are given flexible, mathematically precise definitions within the causal abstraction framework.
A wide range of mechanistic interpretability methods (e.g., activation patching, causal scrubbing, sparse autoencoders, steering) and behavioral interpretability methods (e.g., LIME, integrated gradients) are unified under the common language of causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction provides a theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, the field concerned with providing intelligible algorithms that are faithful simplifications of the known, but opaque low-level details of black box AI models. Our contributions are (1) generalizing the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement (i.e., hard and soft interventions) to arbitrary mechanism transformation (i.e., functionals from old mechanisms to new mechanisms), (2) providing a flexible, yet precise formalization for the core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness, and (3) unifying a variety of mechanistic interpretability methods in the common language of causal abstraction, namely, activation and path patching, causal mediation analysis, causal scrubbing, causal tracing, circuit analysis, concept erasure, sparse autoencoders, differential binary masking, distributed alignment search, and steering.

papers.title: Explainability Techniques for Chemical Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: CorrSteer: Generation-Time LLM Steering via Correlated Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we effectively steer large language models using Sparse Autoencoder features without requiring contrastive datasets or large activation storage?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CorrSteer, a fully automated pipeline that selects task-relevant Sparse Autoencoder features by correlating generation-time activations with task outcomes, and uses these features to steer model behavior with reduced side effects.
papers.conclusion: CorrSteer establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across diverse language model applications.
papers.key_findings:
CorrSteer improves performance on QA, bias mitigation, and safety benchmarks, e.g., +3.3% on MMLU and +27.2% on HarmBench.
Correlation-based feature selection is effective and scalable, requiring only inference-time activations and no contrastive data.
Multi-layer steering (CorrSteer-A, CorrSteer-P) outperforms single-feature steering, suggesting collaborative circuit effects.
CorrSteer reduces side effects compared to fine-tuning, as measured by the Side Effect Ratio (SER).
Selected features are semantically interpretable and align with task requirements (e.g., refusal features for safety, structured output for multiple-choice).
papers.limitation:
CorrSteer is static and cannot easily adapt to dynamic tasks or separate benign from harmful requests without additional context.
The method may capture spurious correlations rather than causal relationships, especially with limited samples.
future_direction: Extend CorrSteer to dynamic tasks and sequential decision-making.
Improve feature selection to further reduce spurious correlations.
Apply the method to larger models and more complex domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable features from large language models (LLMs) without supervision. However, their effectiveness in downstream steering tasks is limited by the requirement for contrastive datasets or large activation storage. To address these limitations, we propose CorrSteer, which selects features by correlating sample correctness with SAE activations from generated tokens at inference time. This approach uses only inference-time activations to extract more relevant features, thereby reducing spurious correlations. It also obtains steering coefficients from average activations, automating the entire pipeline. Our method shows improved task performance on QA, bias mitigation, jailbreaking prevention, and reasoning benchmarks on Gemma-2 2B and LLaMA-3.1 8B, notably achieving a +3.3% improvement in MMLU performance with 4000 samples and a +27.2% improvement in HarmBench with only 108 samples. Selected features demonstrate semantically meaningful patterns aligned with each task's requirements, revealing the underlying capabilities that drive performance. Our work establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across language model applications.

papers.title: Feature Extraction and Steering for Enhanced Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How to enhance the reasoning ability of LLMs without external datasets by extracting features from vanilla Chain-of-Thought and steering internal states?
papers.core_contribution: A framework that extracts reasoning features from vanilla CoT via verbal/symbolic decomposition and steers LLM activations to enhance reasoning without external datasets or retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed feature extraction and steering methods enhance reasoning in LLMs, and the SAE-free approach extends the benefits to models without corresponding SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based steering improves accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
SAE-free steering works without pre-trained SAEs and achieves comparable or better performance.
Steering increases reasoning length and attention to mathematical tokens.
There is an optimal steering strength; too high strength degrades performance.
The method suppresses noisy features and amplifies task-relevant reasoning features.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to mathematical reasoning datasets.
Experiments are limited to three model families (LLaMA, DeepSeek, Gemma).
future_direction: Extend to more diverse reasoning domains such as logical reasoning, scientific problem-solving, or multi-step planning.
Apply the method to more diverse LLM architectures to verify generalizability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate the ability to solve reasoning and mathematical problems using the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) technique. Expanding CoT length, as seen in models such as DeepSeek-R1, significantly enhances this reasoning for complex problems, but requires costly and high-quality long CoT data and fine-tuning. This work, inspired by the deep thinking paradigm of DeepSeek-R1, utilizes a steering technique to enhance the reasoning ability of an LLM without external datasets. Our method first employs Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract interpretable features from vanilla CoT. These features are then used to steer the LLM's internal states during generation. Recognizing that many LLMs do not have corresponding pre-trained SAEs, we further introduce a novel SAE-free steering algorithm, which directly computes steering directions from the residual activations of an LLM, obviating the need for an explicit SAE. Experimental results demonstrate that both our SAE-based and subsequent SAE-free steering algorithms significantly enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: Analyze Feature Flow to Enhance Interpretation and Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do features discovered by sparse autoencoders evolve across consecutive layers of large language models, and how can this understanding be used for interpretability and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a data-free cosine similarity method to map Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across transformer layers, creating flow graphs that reveal feature evolution and enable precise model steering through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-layer feature mapping framework provides granular interpretability of feature evolution in LLMs and offers a new, transparent method for steering model behavior through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Cosine similarity between SAE decoder weights effectively identifies feature relationships across layers, validated against activation correlations.
Feature formation follows distinct patterns: early layers show high entropy and feature birth, middle layers stabilize, and later layers primarily propagate existing features.
Deactivating predecessor features identified by the top-1 cosine match is causally effective, outperforming random selection.
Multi-layer steering using flow graphs is more effective and less sensitive to hyperparameters than single-layer interventions.
Flow graphs provide mechanistic insights, revealing how semantic meaning (e.g., 'particle physics') evolves and transforms across the model's computational pathway.
papers.limitation: The current steering procedure operates locally on hidden states and may not fully redirect the model's computational trajectory to a different 'minima' for truly efficient deactivation or activation.
future_direction: Further research on flow graphs as a unit of study for model interpretability.
Extending the steering experiments and flow graph analysis to other model architectures like Llama Scope.
Investigating the method's applicability and performance across a wider range of models and SAE training configurations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new approach to systematically map features discovered by sparse autoencoder across consecutive layers of large language models, extending earlier work that examined inter-layer feature links. By using a data-free cosine similarity technique, we trace how specific features persist, transform, or first appear at each stage. This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Toward a Flexible Framework for Linear Representation Hypothesis Using Maximum Likelihood Estimation
papers.research_question: How can we generalize the linear representation hypothesis to handle complex, context-dependent concepts without relying on single-token counterfactual pairs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generalized framework that redefines binary concepts as unit vectors in a canonical representation space and uses activation differences formalized via a von Mises-Fisher distribution and maximum likelihood estimation to compute concept directions, eliminating the need for single-token counterfactual pairs.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a generalized framework that bridges linear representation hypothesis and representation engineering, offering a principled and robust method for constructing concept directions that is lightweight, flexible, and effective for monitoring and manipulating LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SAND method consistently outperforms PCA and zero-shot baselines in monitoring truthfulness and other QA tasks across LLaMA models.
SAND accurately captures concept directions (e.g., for gender, case, language) for steering interventions, whereas PCA fails in some cases.
SAND is computationally efficient, requiring only one matrix multiplication, making it lightweight and easy to integrate into existing activation engineering pipelines.
The method provides theoretical justification for the empirical effectiveness of the heuristic Mean Difference method for extracting steering vectors.
The framework bridges the gap between the theory of linear representation hypothesis and the practice of representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Linear representation hypothesis posits that high-level concepts are encoded as linear directions in the representation spaces of LLMs. Park et al. (2024) formalize this notion by unifying multiple interpretations of linear representation, such as 1-dimensional subspace representation and interventions, using a causal inner product. However, their framework relies on single-token counterfactual pairs and cannot handle ambiguous contrasting pairs, limiting its applicability to complex or context-dependent concepts. We introduce a new notion of binary concepts as unit vectors in a canonical representation space, and utilize LLMs' (neural) activation differences along with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to compute concept directions (i.e., steering vectors). Our method, Sum of Activation-base Normalized Difference (SAND), formalizes the use of activation differences modeled as samples from a von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution, providing a principled approach to derive concept directions. We extend the applicability of Park et al. (2024) by eliminating the dependency on unembedding representations and single-token pairs. Through experiments with LLaMA models across diverse concepts and benchmarks, we demonstrate that our lightweight approach offers greater flexibility, superior performance in activation engineering tasks like monitoring and manipulation.

papers.title: Scaling laws for activation steering with Llama 2 models and refusal mechanisms
papers.research_question: How does the effectiveness of the Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering technique scale with model size, specifically for controlling refusal behavior in Llama 2 models?
papers.core_contribution: The effectiveness of Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) for steering model behavior diminishes with increasing model size, negative steering is more effective than positive steering, and steering is most effective when applied at early-mid layers.
papers.conclusion: Model alignment is complex and requires nuanced approaches to steer models effectively as they become larger, with future research needed to understand the interplay between alignment strategies, model architecture, and dataset characteristics.
papers.key_findings:
CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers (approximately 0.4 × total layer count).
The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size, making larger models harder to steer with the same vectors.
Negative steering (towards non-refusal) has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.
The layer of peak steering effectiveness for positive and negative steering converges as model size increases.
The diminishing effectiveness might be because larger models 'drown out' the steering vector due to more downstream computation.
papers.limitation: The experiments were limited to the specific topic of refusal and the results may be different for different topics or prompting approaches.
future_direction: Feature steering with sparse autoencoders (SAE).
Modifying activation steering for larger models, e.g., scaling up steering vectors or injecting at multiple layers.
Experimenting with diverse model architectures (e.g., Mistral, BERT, BLOOM) to understand alignment differences.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve in complexity and capability, the efficacy of less widely deployed alignment techniques are uncertain. Building on previous work on activation steering and contrastive activation addition (CAA), this paper explores the effectiveness of CAA with model scale using the family of Llama 2 models (7B, 13B, and 70B). CAA works by finding desirable 'directions' in the model's residual stream vector space using contrastive pairs (for example, hate to love) and adding this direction to the residual stream during the forward pass. It directly manipulates the residual stream and aims to extract features from language models to better control their outputs. Using answer matching questions centered around the refusal behavior, we found that 1) CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers. 2) The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size. 3) Negative steering has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.

papers.title: Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can content biases in reasoning be mitigated through activation steering in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-CAST, a fine-grained conditional activation steering method that effectively reduces content biases in reasoning, improving formal reasoning accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.conclusion: Activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive steering methods enable linear control over content biases in reasoning.
Static steering is insufficient to debias all tested models.
K-CAST reduces biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.
Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations and incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities.
Steering vectors can partially generalize to different out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are performed on LLMs of up to 9 billion parameters due to computational constraints.
The study focuses mainly on synthetically generated tasks, which may not fully capture real-world applications.
future_direction: Applying the steering methodology to larger models.
Assessing how steering for content effect can impact real-world applications in critical domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently demonstrate reasoning limitations, often conflating content plausibility (i.e., material inference) with logical validity (i.e., formal inference). This can result in biased inferences, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa. Mitigating this limitation is critical, as it undermines the trustworthiness and generalizability of LLMs in applications that demand rigorous logical consistency. This paper investigates the problem of mitigating content biases on formal reasoning through activation steering. Specifically, we curate a controlled syllogistic reasoning dataset to disentangle formal validity from content plausibility. After localising the layers responsible for formal and material inference, we investigate contrastive activation steering methods for test-time interventions. An extensive empirical analysis on different LLMs reveals that contrastive steering consistently supports linear control over content biases. However, we observe that a static approach is insufficient for improving all the tested models. We then leverage the possibility to control content effects by dynamically determining the value of the steering parameters via fine-grained conditional methods. We found that conditional steering is effective on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy with a newly introduced kNN-based method (K-CAST). Finally, additional experiments reveal that steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Practically, this paper demonstrates that activation-level interventions can offer a scalable strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased formal reasoning.

papers.title: Multi-property Steering of Large Language Models with Dynamic Activation Composition
papers.research_question: How can activation steering methods be optimized for multi-property conditioning while maintaining generation fluency?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Dynamic Activation Composition, an information-theoretic approach to dynamically adjust steering intensity for multi-property conditioning, improving fluency and conditioning strength.
papers.conclusion: The Dynamic Activation Composition method successfully maintains high conditioning while minimizing the impact on generation fluency for multi-property steering.
papers.key_findings:
Start strategy fails to maintain conditioning throughout generation.
Fixed and Dim strategies can lead to disfluencies at high steering intensities.
Negative steering effectively conditions against properties.
Dynamic Activation Composition achieves the best trade-off between conditioning and fluency in multi-property settings.
Steering vectors for related languages show similar patterns.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods were shown to be effective in conditioning language model generation by additively intervening over models' intermediate representations. However, the evaluation of these techniques has so far been limited to single conditioning properties and synthetic settings. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various activation steering strategies, highlighting the property-dependent nature of optimal parameters to ensure a robust effect throughout generation. To address this issue, we propose Dynamic Activation Composition, an information-theoretic approach to modulate the steering intensity of one or more properties throughout generation. Our experiments on multi-property steering show that our method successfully maintains high conditioning while minimizing the impact of conditioning on generation fluency.

papers.title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Whether in-context learning and activation steering are instances of a broader framework for controlling LLM behavior, and how they jointly affect model behavior.
papers.core_contribution: Presents a Bayesian belief dynamics model that unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior under both interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Bayesian belief dynamics model unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior and revealing a phase boundary between interventions.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning and activation steering jointly affect behavior, creating a phase boundary modulated by context and activations.
The Bayesian model predicts sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates and additivity of interventions in log-belief space.
The model predicts crossover points (N*) where behavior transitions between concepts, with high correlation to empirical data.
The linear representation hypothesis holds within a range of steering magnitudes, beyond which behavior breaks down.
The model generalizes across different LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets (persona, sentiment).
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis breaks down with large steering magnitudes, leading to chance behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be controlled at inference time through prompts (in-context learning) and internal activations (activation steering). Different accounts have been proposed to explain these methods, yet their common goal of controlling model behavior raises the question of whether these seemingly disparate methodologies can be seen as specific instances of a broader framework. Motivated by this, we develop a unifying, predictive account of LLM control from a Bayesian perspective. Specifically, we posit that both context- and activation-based interventions impact model behavior by altering its belief in latent concepts: steering operates by changing concept priors, while in-context learning leads to an accumulation of evidence. This results in a closed-form Bayesian model that is highly predictive of LLM behavior across context- and activation-based interventions in a set of domains inspired by prior work on many-shot in-context learning. This model helps us explain prior empirical phenomena - e.g., sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates - while predicting novel ones - e.g., additivity of both interventions in log-belief space, which results in distinct phases such that sudden and dramatic behavioral shifts can be induced by slightly changing intervention controls. Taken together, this work offers a unified account of prompt-based and activation-based control of LLM behavior, and a methodology for empirically predicting the effects of these interventions.

papers.title: Representation Engineering for Large-Language Models: Survey and Research Challenges
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the goals, methods, and challenges of representation engineering as an approach to make large-language models more predictable and controllable.
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes the goals and methods of representation engineering, providing a cohesive survey of this emerging discipline and outlining a research agenda for building more predictable and controllable large-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation engineering is a promising approach for enhancing LLM transparency and control, and it provides a clear agenda for future research to address current challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Representation engineering uses contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations, offering a top-down approach to model interpretability and control.
It compares favorably with alternative approaches like mechanistic interpretability and prompt-engineering in certain aspects.
Risks include performance degradation, increased compute time, and steerability issues.
The linear representation hypothesis underpins representation engineering, but its strong form may not hold, limiting generalizability.
Future research should focus on dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.limitation:
Performance decrease, compute time increases, and steerability issues.
The strong linear representation hypothesis may not hold, limiting generalized interventions.
future_direction: Build predictable, dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large-language models are capable of completing a variety of tasks, but remain unpredictable and intractable. Representation engineering seeks to resolve this problem through a new approach utilizing samples of contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations of concepts such as honesty, harmfulness or power-seeking. We formalize the goals and methods of representation engineering to present a cohesive picture of work in this emerging discipline. We compare it with alternative approaches, such as mechanistic interpretability, prompt-engineering and fine-tuning. We outline risks such as performance decrease, compute time increases and steerability issues. We present a clear agenda for future research to build predictable, dynamic, safe and personalizable LLMs.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Integrating clinical reasoning into large language model-based diagnosis through etiology-aware attention steering
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex clinical scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: This study proposes an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework that integrates structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis by identifying and steering attention heads crucial for etiology reasoning, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and reasoning focus.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework integrates etiology-aware attention guidance with authoritative clinical guidelines, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy, attention stability, and reasoning interpretability, holding strong potential for real-world clinical deployment in complex diagnostic environments.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines on the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort.
External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort confirms the framework's effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy in real-world complex scenarios.
The Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm successfully pinpoints attention heads that exhibit strong alignment with etiological reasoning.
Ablation studies demonstrate the importance of each component (CRS annotation, Etiology-Aware Head Identification, Reasoning-Guided Loss) for overall performance.
The framework enhances the model's attention stability and reasoning interpretability across diverse diagnostic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to a broader range of diseases and clinical scenarios.
Integrating multimodal data (e.g., medical images, lab waveforms) to enhance diagnostic reasoning.
Incorporating contrastive or self-supervised objectives to further enhance model robustness in low-resource or noisy environments.
papers.abstract: Objective: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate significant capabilities in medical text understanding and generation. However, their diagnostic reliability in complex clinical scenarios remains limited. This study aims to enhance LLMs' diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability. Method: We propose an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework to integrate structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis. Specifically, we first construct Clinical Reasoning Scaffolding (CRS) based on authoritative clinical guidelines for three representative acute abdominal emergencies: acute appendicitis, acute pancreatitis, and acute cholecystitis. Next, we develop the Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm to pinpoint attention heads crucial for the model's etiology reasoning. To ensure reliable clinical reasoning alignment, we introduce the Reasoning-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning that embeds etiological reasoning cues into input representations and steers the selected Etiology-Aware Heads toward critical information through a Reasoning-Guided Loss function. Result: On the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort, our framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines. External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort further confirms its effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy. Further assessments via Reasoning Attention Frequency indicate that our models exhibit enhanced reliability when faced with real-world complex scenarios. Conclusion: This study presents a practical and effective approach to enhance clinical reasoning in LLM-based diagnosis. By aligning model attention with structured CRS, the proposed framework offers a promising paradigm for building more interpretable and reliable AI diagnostic systems in complex clinical settings.

papers.title: In-Distribution Steering: Balancing Control and Coherence in Language Model Generation
papers.research_question: How can we balance behavioral control and text coherence in language model generation by dynamically adjusting activation steering strength based on the input's position within the target behavior's activation distribution?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces In-Distribution Steering (IDS), a novel activation steering method that dynamically adjusts intervention strength per input to achieve precise behavioral control while maintaining the plausibility and coherence of generated text.
papers.conclusion: IDS enables fine-grained control over LLM behavior while maintaining output quality, making it a practical tool for deploying more controllable and reliable language models in high-stakes applications.
papers.key_findings:
IDS achieves superior Steering Performance Impact (SPI) compared to competitors (CAA, MERA) across diverse models and datasets, ranking first on average.
IDS maintains text plausibility (perplexity) close to baseline methods while avoiding the collapse and non-plausible text generated by over-steering competitors like MERA.
IDS operates along the Pareto frontier between steering performance and text plausibility, demonstrating an optimal trade-off.
